medical.title: Stroke diagnosis improved by AI support, multinational study finds
medical.summary: Dr. Chi Kyung (CK) Kim of the Department of Neurology at Korea University Guro Hospital and his research team successfully conducted a multinational validation of AI technology that precisely detects large vessel occlusion (LVO) in acute stroke patients using only standard brain CT (non-contrast CT) without contrast agents. The findings are published in the Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery. The team includes research Dr. Kim Beom-joon of the Department of Neurology, Dr. Jun Sun-woo of the Department of Radiology at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, and CMO Ryu Wi-sun of JLK.

medical.title: Nationwide safety program associated with 65% reduction in hospital-onset MRSA bloodstream infections
medical.summary: A large-scale, quality improvement program developed in collaboration with infection prevention experts at the Johns Hopkins Armstrong Institute for Patient Safety and Quality was associated with a 65% reduction in hospital-onset bloodstream infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) among participating hospital units.

medical.title: Potential new TB vaccines could save millions of lives: Gavi
medical.summary: New tuberculosis vaccines expected to become available from 2029 could save more than 7 million lives over a decade, Gavi said Monday, but only if sufficient supply is ensured for the countries most in need.

medical.title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals trade-off between glucose control and daily well-being
medical.summary: New research to be presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, shows that among people living with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, data from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices paired with daily quality-of-life ratings found that days with more widely fluctuating glucose readings (while still within safe limits) were followed by days with better quality of life than days with stricter control—suggesting the burden of stricter control could prevent individuals from enjoying various activities.

medical.title: Smartphone-controlled microneedle patch could offer drug-free pain care from afar
medical.summary: A "wearable electroceutical" has been developed that could reduce the need to visit a hospital or rely on painkillers every time pain occurs. When attached to the skin, it modulates pain through electrical stimulation and can be remotely controlled via smartphone even across long distances, such as between Korea and the United States.

medical.title: Researchers say parents should combine words with gestures to help their children learn
medical.summary: As children return to school, new research from the University of Iowa shows how parents can help their kids learn while literally being on the same wavelength.

medical.title: Time-restricted eating provides modest weight loss benefits for adults with obesity and prediabetes
medical.summary: A Johns Hopkins Medicine study reports evidence that time-restricted eating (TRE)—a form of intermittent fasting that involves eating only during a consistent daily 8–10-hour window—can cause modest weight loss in adults with obesity and prediabetes or diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.

medical.title: Common epilepsy drug levetiracetam presents potential clot risk for patients taking blood thinners
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of Liverpool and the University of Zurich have identified a potential safety consideration involving levetiracetam, one of the world's most commonly prescribed antiseizure medications.

medical.title: Promising new option for skin cancer reconstruction uses hydrogel-based template
medical.summary: Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified a promising approach to rebuilding tissue after skin cancer surgery that could help some patients avoid more extensive reconstructive procedures.

medical.title: Lymphatic vessels use Reelin protein to help regulate embryonic heart growth
medical.summary: A Northwestern Medicine study has uncovered a previously unknown signaling system that helps regulate heart growth during development, according to the study published in the journal Genes & Development.

medical.title: How changes in prefrontal brain activity can impair the ability to change behavior
medical.summary: A new study has revealed how both reduced neural activity and reduced control over neural activity in the brain's prefrontal area can disrupt the ability to adapt behavior when circumstances change.

medical.title: UK-wide rectal cancer study helps improve radiotherapy standards across the country
medical.summary: A major UK-wide cancer study has helped establish new standards for planning and delivering radiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, benefiting patients across the UK, including those in northeast Scotland.

medical.title: New framework identifies 108 lysosomal disorders, nearly doubling recognized conditions
medical.summary: Lysosomal disorders can have devastating effects on patients but findings from a University of Sheffield-led collaborative study could support more precise diagnosis and help researchers identify shared targets for future treatments. The scientists have brought together the most comprehensive picture yet of rare metabolic disorders, identifying 108 conditions—almost double those originally understood to exist—bringing new hope for early diagnosis and new treatments.

medical.title: Newly found dendrite bottlenecks may reshape how neurons handle information
medical.summary: Neurons receive thousands of signals via tree-like extensions called dendrites. Until now, these dendrites were thought to be relatively smooth cables that conduct electrical signals to the cell body. An international research team led by University Hospital of Bonn (UKB), the University of Bonn and the DZNE has determined that this picture is incomplete.

medical.title: Miniaturized bone marrow-on-a-chip tracks human immune cells as they build lasting antibody defenses
medical.summary: A scientific team has developed a laboratory model that reveals how antibody-producing plasma cells migrate, mature and survive within human bone marrow, a main location of long-lived antibody-producing plasma cells. The platform combines a lymph node-mimicking organoid with a tissue chip that mimics bone marrow, allowing scientists to observe key stages of plasma cell development that have been difficult to study in humans.

medical.title: Examining the neural basis of socially anxious behaviors
medical.summary: People with social anxiety are especially sensitive to unpleasant outcomes, and this sensitivity contributes to their tendency to avoid social situations. Previous research has linked this learning bias to activity in specific brain regions. Hanjie Liu and Melle van der Molen of Leiden University extended this work by examining how communication between brain regions coordinates learning behavior in people with varying levels of social anxiety.

medical.title: Young military veterans have higher 'forever chemical' levels than non-veterans
medical.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), often called forever chemicals because of their long-lasting presence in humans and the environment, are commonly found in consumer and industrial products. When Brown University researchers examined PFAS levels in the blood serum of U.S. military veterans, they found that younger veterans had higher PFAS concentrations and a higher prevalence of elevated PFAS levels compared with civilians of similar ages.

medical.title: Early deafness may reshape the brain to devote more resources to peripheral vision
medical.summary: People with intact hearing can use sound as an alert system for events outside their direct line of sight. This seemingly puts those who have lost their hearing at a disadvantage. However, according to a new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the brains of people who lose their hearing at an early age may compensate by devoting more resources to developing better peripheral vision.

medical.title: Metabolic vulnerability identified that may affect heart development
medical.summary: The heart undergoes major changes during the first weeks of life. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet have now shown that a previously unknown metabolic vulnerability in mitochondria can disrupt heart development. The study, published in Science Advances, could improve our understanding of rare mitochondrial diseases that affect the heart.

medical.title: Why so few older Americans get counseling—and how it could help
medical.summary: People are living longer, reshaping what it means to grow old. By the late 2060s, an estimated 2.5 billion people worldwide will be 60 or older—more than the number of people who are under 18. The population ages 80 and older is expected to grow even faster, more than tripling between 2023 and 2060 to about 545 million.

medical.title: Engineered vesicles protect brain from bacterial toxin
medical.summary: Bacterial meningitis can cause severe brain damage even when patients receive antibiotic treatment promptly. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet have developed tiny biological vesicles that, in animal studies, were able to capture bacterial toxins, protect neurons, reduce inflammation and delay disease progression. The findings are published in the journal Journal of Extracellular Vesicles.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
medical.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

medical.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
medical.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

medical.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
medical.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

science.title: Economists examine how people infer, revise beliefs in face of new information
science.summary: When people hear something new about a topic, they should update their beliefs to reflect the new information. But many people either underreact or overreact, with their responses varying based on different factors, including the environment. In "The Inference-Forecast Gap in Belief Updating," researchers compared how people make inferences and revise their beliefs in light of the same information.

science.title: Peptide position determines whether gold nanoparticles branch or stay spherical
science.summary: The position of biomineralization peptides within liposomes can influence how gold nanoparticles grow, reports a research team from the Institute of Science Tokyo. Peptides localized at the membrane interface promote branched structures, while those confined to the liposome interior favor spherical nanoparticles. The findings offer a new strategy for controlling nanoscale reaction environments in nanoparticle synthesis.

science.title: Unused natural gas behind NYC's $300 million waste of a potent greenhouse gas
science.summary: Methane emissions from the New York City metropolitan area are largely driven by natural gas use, according to a new study published today in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics by researchers at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, part of the Columbia Climate School. The findings may offer cities an overlooked pathway for reducing methane emissions while potentially saving consumers millions of dollars lost to wasted natural gas.

science.title: Only 1 out of every 5 amphibian type localities in Ecuador are in protected areas
science.summary: In taxonomy, the location where specimens used to formally describe a new species are collected is called a type locality. These sites can be thought of as the species' formal birthplace, much as the scientific article containing the original description constitutes its scientific birth certificate, because this is how the species officially acquires its identity and name within the scientific community.

science.title: A painting signed 'L daVinci': Analysis reveals Renaissance pigments and later alterations
science.summary: Researchers at Uppsala University have analyzed the color pigments in a historical painting signed "L daVinci." Most of the pigments are consistent with materials used during the Renaissance, while a more recent pigment appears to be linked to later alterations. The study demonstrates how materials science can provide new pieces of the puzzle behind the history of a work of art.

science.title: Neutral radicals unlock porous organic semiconductors without chemical doping
science.summary: Researchers at the Center for Research in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Materials (CiQUS) at the Universidade de Santiago de Compostela (USC) have developed a new strategy for producing covalent organic frameworks (COFs) with semiconducting properties without relying on chemical doping. The approach could open new avenues for developing materials for applications in electronics and energy storage.

science.title: Mapping charge-carrier dynamics to guide more efficient organic solar cells
science.summary: A Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) research team led by professors Taeyeon Kim and Doo-Hyun Ko of the Department of Chemistry recently published a comprehensive review titled "Carrier Dynamics in Nonfullerene Acceptor Organic Photovoltaics through Ultrafast Spectroscopy" in the journal ACS Nano.

science.title: New Crops, Health Research Proposals to Help NASA Advance Exploration
science.summary: NASA has selected 12 new investigations to help support human explorers in space. Six will help advance the ability to produce food off-planet, while another six advance the understanding of how unique conditions associated with space exploration can impact the health and physiology of astronauts. The six food-focused investigations, supported by the agency’s Space […]

science.title: Cancer-linked protein binds to chromosome in unexpected way, study finds
science.summary: A new 3D structure of a cancer-linked protein bound to its cellular partner reveals details of how the protein binds to chromosomes and could offer insights for future disease treatments. The protein—BRD4—plays a critical role in how cells read, copy and repair DNA and helps determine how different kinds of cells are made; it has been linked to many types of cancer and is considered a promising target for future therapies. The study, led by scientists at Penn State and published in the journal Molecular Cell, found that BRD4 can attach to DNA-packaging structures in cells even without a molecular signal long believed to be necessary for the interaction.

science.title: 40-year-old prediction of how plastics 'mix' confirmed for the first time
science.summary: A "mixing" phenomenon between plastic layers that had been predicted only in theory for 40 years has now been experimentally confirmed.

science.title: Rivers may be carrying more microplastics into the world's oceans than previously thought
science.summary: Microplastics are a modern environmental menace and a potential threat to human health. These tiny pieces of plastic, measuring from 1 to 5,000 micrometers, come mainly from larger plastics as well as sources such as paints and cosmetics. They are found in almost every corner of the planet, and a new study published in Science suggests rivers may be carrying far more of them into the ocean than previously thought.

science.title: Series of reactions reveals how complex carbon chemistry can begin in frigid space
science.summary: Before there was Earth, there was chemistry. In the unimaginable cold, dark clouds where stars and planets are born, carbon molecules assemble into more complex forms—starting a chemical journey that could eventually deliver some of life's basic ingredients to young planets. There's only one problem: These molecules need heat to form. At least that's what scientists have long believed. But new research from FIU chemist Alexander Mebel reveals such chemistry can actually happen at temperatures nearing absolute zero, which is -460°F (-273°C).

science.title: Salicornia genomes reveal genetic secrets to farming on salty land
science.summary: A University of Newcastle-led global study has produced the most complete genetic picture yet of a salt-loving plant with the potential to help grow food in some of the world's harshest environments.

science.title: Striving for perfection could impact well-being of gifted youth
science.summary: The pressure to be perfect may intensify for kids once they get into high school—especially for those labeled as "gifted," according to a new University of Georgia study published in Gifted Child Quarterly.

science.title: How chronic absenteeism shifted in Canadian kindergarten after COVID‑19
science.summary: Kindergarten is an important time in a child's life, during which children acquire and strengthen the skills needed to participate and learn in a school environment. Going to school regularly is an important part of this.

science.title: Social isolation in Australia has nearly doubled over two decades
science.summary: Australians are becoming increasingly lonely and socially isolated, according to new University of Sydney research that found rates of social isolation nearly doubled over the past 23 years. Loneliness rates also increased over time, though more gradually than social isolation, with the sharpest impacts observed among vulnerable populations.

science.title: Mosquito 'toilet' detects West Nile and first Hedwig-like virus found in the Americas
science.summary: When public health researchers want to know whether diseases such as COVID-19 or polio are circulating in a community, they can look for genetic evidence in wastewater.

science.title: Speedy electrons for brilliant laser light: Research paves the way for compact, inexpensive free-electron lasers
science.summary: Extremely short, intense light flashes are in high demand to investigate atoms, molecules and new materials. Free-electron lasers (FELs) produce these flashes. But around the world, beam time available at large-scale user facilities is in short supply, and waiting times are long.

science.title: School segregation endures in Baltimore region, report finds
science.summary: Although public schools in Baltimore City are predominantly Black, the district is doing a better job of reducing segregation among its student body than suburban systems that are able to draw from more diverse populations, according to a new report from Johns Hopkins University.

science.title: AI updates can sometimes feel like breakups or losses, study finds
science.summary: Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language.

science.title: NASA Welcomes Djibouti as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
science.summary: The Republic of Djibouti became the 72nd nation and eighth African country to sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony Monday at NASA Headquarters in Washington. The Artemis Accords are the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing transparency, safety, and coordination among nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. “Djibouti joins […]

science.title: Gender representation key to women's job interest, study suggests
science.summary: Women make up about half the U.S. population, yet remain a minority in many professions, such as politics, technology, science and academia.

science.title: Ghana's local architecture has adapted to change for centuries. It can teach us about climate resilience
science.summary: When people discuss architecture in Ghana, attention often focuses on modern buildings: concrete houses, glass offices, shopping malls and ambitious urban developments. Yet across the country, another architectural tradition continues to offer lessons about how people have built and lived for generations.

science.title: Getting photons into shape for reliable quantum communication
science.summary: The vast majority of modern quantum technologies—from quantum cryptography to the quantum internet to the quantum computer—rely on one essential element: the transmission of photons. Two qubits (two atoms, for example) exchange information: One qubit emits a photon, and the other qubit absorbs it.

science.title: How the 2024 solar superstorm drained Earth's radiation belt
science.summary: In May 2024, Earth experienced its most intense geomagnetic storm since the Halloween storms of 2003. This "superstorm" filled night skies in many parts of the world with colorful aurorae, and it disrupted some infrastructure, such as GPS signals used by agricultural equipment.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: Primarul municipiului Focşani, Cristi Valentin Misăilă, le cere părinţilor să nu contribuie cu bani la aşa-numitul „fond al clasei” sau pentru cumpărarea de materiale didactice şi produse necesare în unităţile de învăţământ, susţinând că şcolile au fondurile necesare pentru funcţionare.

mix_items.summary: Rareș a învățat să creadă în propriile puteri datorită sprijinului educațional și emoțional oferit de Fundația Inocenți. Descoperă povestea lui. The post Rareș, băiatul care a învățat să creadă în propriile puteri appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Economists examine how people infer, revise beliefs in face of new information
mix_items.summary: When people hear something new about a topic, they should update their beliefs to reflect the new information. But many people either underreact or overreact, with their responses varying based on different factors, including the environment. In "The Inference-Forecast Gap in Belief Updating," researchers compared how people make inferences and revise their beliefs in light of the same information.

mix_items.title: Peptide position determines whether gold nanoparticles branch or stay spherical
mix_items.summary: The position of biomineralization peptides within liposomes can influence how gold nanoparticles grow, reports a research team from the Institute of Science Tokyo. Peptides localized at the membrane interface promote branched structures, while those confined to the liposome interior favor spherical nanoparticles. The findings offer a new strategy for controlling nanoscale reaction environments in nanoparticle synthesis.

mix_items.title: Stroke diagnosis improved by AI support, multinational study finds
mix_items.summary: Dr. Chi Kyung (CK) Kim of the Department of Neurology at Korea University Guro Hospital and his research team successfully conducted a multinational validation of AI technology that precisely detects large vessel occlusion (LVO) in acute stroke patients using only standard brain CT (non-contrast CT) without contrast agents. The findings are published in the Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery. The team includes research Dr. Kim Beom-joon of the Department of Neurology, Dr. Jun Sun-woo of the Department of Radiology at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, and CMO Ryu Wi-sun of JLK.

mix_items.title: Nationwide safety program associated with 65% reduction in hospital-onset MRSA bloodstream infections
mix_items.summary: A large-scale, quality improvement program developed in collaboration with infection prevention experts at the Johns Hopkins Armstrong Institute for Patient Safety and Quality was associated with a 65% reduction in hospital-onset bloodstream infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) among participating hospital units.

mix_items.title: Unused natural gas behind NYC's $300 million waste of a potent greenhouse gas
mix_items.summary: Methane emissions from the New York City metropolitan area are largely driven by natural gas use, according to a new study published today in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics by researchers at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, part of the Columbia Climate School. The findings may offer cities an overlooked pathway for reducing methane emissions while potentially saving consumers millions of dollars lost to wasted natural gas.

mix_items.title: Only 1 out of every 5 amphibian type localities in Ecuador are in protected areas
mix_items.summary: In taxonomy, the location where specimens used to formally describe a new species are collected is called a type locality. These sites can be thought of as the species' formal birthplace, much as the scientific article containing the original description constitutes its scientific birth certificate, because this is how the species officially acquires its identity and name within the scientific community.

mix_items.title: A painting signed 'L daVinci': Analysis reveals Renaissance pigments and later alterations
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Uppsala University have analyzed the color pigments in a historical painting signed "L daVinci." Most of the pigments are consistent with materials used during the Renaissance, while a more recent pigment appears to be linked to later alterations. The study demonstrates how materials science can provide new pieces of the puzzle behind the history of a work of art.

mix_items.title: Neutral radicals unlock porous organic semiconductors without chemical doping
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Center for Research in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Materials (CiQUS) at the Universidade de Santiago de Compostela (USC) have developed a new strategy for producing covalent organic frameworks (COFs) with semiconducting properties without relying on chemical doping. The approach could open new avenues for developing materials for applications in electronics and energy storage.

mix_items.title: Potential new TB vaccines could save millions of lives: Gavi
mix_items.summary: New tuberculosis vaccines expected to become available from 2029 could save more than 7 million lives over a decade, Gavi said Monday, but only if sufficient supply is ensured for the countries most in need.

mix_items.title: Mapping charge-carrier dynamics to guide more efficient organic solar cells
mix_items.summary: A Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) research team led by professors Taeyeon Kim and Doo-Hyun Ko of the Department of Chemistry recently published a comprehensive review titled "Carrier Dynamics in Nonfullerene Acceptor Organic Photovoltaics through Ultrafast Spectroscopy" in the journal ACS Nano.

mix_items.title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals trade-off between glucose control and daily well-being
mix_items.summary: New research to be presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, shows that among people living with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, data from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices paired with daily quality-of-life ratings found that days with more widely fluctuating glucose readings (while still within safe limits) were followed by days with better quality of life than days with stricter control—suggesting the burden of stricter control could prevent individuals from enjoying various activities.

mix_items.title: Smartphone-controlled microneedle patch could offer drug-free pain care from afar
mix_items.summary: A "wearable electroceutical" has been developed that could reduce the need to visit a hospital or rely on painkillers every time pain occurs. When attached to the skin, it modulates pain through electrical stimulation and can be remotely controlled via smartphone even across long distances, such as between Korea and the United States.

mix_items.title: Researchers say parents should combine words with gestures to help their children learn
mix_items.summary: As children return to school, new research from the University of Iowa shows how parents can help their kids learn while literally being on the same wavelength.

mix_items.title: New Crops, Health Research Proposals to Help NASA Advance Exploration
mix_items.summary: NASA has selected 12 new investigations to help support human explorers in space. Six will help advance the ability to produce food off-planet, while another six advance the understanding of how unique conditions associated with space exploration can impact the health and physiology of astronauts. The six food-focused investigations, supported by the agency’s Space […]

mix_items.title: Time-restricted eating provides modest weight loss benefits for adults with obesity and prediabetes
mix_items.summary: A Johns Hopkins Medicine study reports evidence that time-restricted eating (TRE)—a form of intermittent fasting that involves eating only during a consistent daily 8–10-hour window—can cause modest weight loss in adults with obesity and prediabetes or diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.

mix_items.title: Common epilepsy drug levetiracetam presents potential clot risk for patients taking blood thinners
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Liverpool and the University of Zurich have identified a potential safety consideration involving levetiracetam, one of the world's most commonly prescribed antiseizure medications.

mix_items.title: Cancer-linked protein binds to chromosome in unexpected way, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new 3D structure of a cancer-linked protein bound to its cellular partner reveals details of how the protein binds to chromosomes and could offer insights for future disease treatments. The protein—BRD4—plays a critical role in how cells read, copy and repair DNA and helps determine how different kinds of cells are made; it has been linked to many types of cancer and is considered a promising target for future therapies. The study, led by scientists at Penn State and published in the journal Molecular Cell, found that BRD4 can attach to DNA-packaging structures in cells even without a molecular signal long believed to be necessary for the interaction.

mix_items.title: Promising new option for skin cancer reconstruction uses hydrogel-based template
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified a promising approach to rebuilding tissue after skin cancer surgery that could help some patients avoid more extensive reconstructive procedures.

mix_items.title: 40-year-old prediction of how plastics 'mix' confirmed for the first time
mix_items.summary: A "mixing" phenomenon between plastic layers that had been predicted only in theory for 40 years has now been experimentally confirmed.

mix_items.title: Rivers may be carrying more microplastics into the world's oceans than previously thought
mix_items.summary: Microplastics are a modern environmental menace and a potential threat to human health. These tiny pieces of plastic, measuring from 1 to 5,000 micrometers, come mainly from larger plastics as well as sources such as paints and cosmetics. They are found in almost every corner of the planet, and a new study published in Science suggests rivers may be carrying far more of them into the ocean than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Series of reactions reveals how complex carbon chemistry can begin in frigid space
mix_items.summary: Before there was Earth, there was chemistry. In the unimaginable cold, dark clouds where stars and planets are born, carbon molecules assemble into more complex forms—starting a chemical journey that could eventually deliver some of life's basic ingredients to young planets. There's only one problem: These molecules need heat to form. At least that's what scientists have long believed. But new research from FIU chemist Alexander Mebel reveals such chemistry can actually happen at temperatures nearing absolute zero, which is -460°F (-273°C).

mix_items.title: Lymphatic vessels use Reelin protein to help regulate embryonic heart growth
mix_items.summary: A Northwestern Medicine study has uncovered a previously unknown signaling system that helps regulate heart growth during development, according to the study published in the journal Genes & Development.

mix_items.title: How changes in prefrontal brain activity can impair the ability to change behavior
mix_items.summary: A new study has revealed how both reduced neural activity and reduced control over neural activity in the brain's prefrontal area can disrupt the ability to adapt behavior when circumstances change.

mix_items.title: Salicornia genomes reveal genetic secrets to farming on salty land
mix_items.summary: A University of Newcastle-led global study has produced the most complete genetic picture yet of a salt-loving plant with the potential to help grow food in some of the world's harshest environments.

mix_items.title: UK-wide rectal cancer study helps improve radiotherapy standards across the country
mix_items.summary: A major UK-wide cancer study has helped establish new standards for planning and delivering radiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, benefiting patients across the UK, including those in northeast Scotland.

mix_items.title: Striving for perfection could impact well-being of gifted youth
mix_items.summary: The pressure to be perfect may intensify for kids once they get into high school—especially for those labeled as "gifted," according to a new University of Georgia study published in Gifted Child Quarterly.

mix_items.title: How chronic absenteeism shifted in Canadian kindergarten after COVID‑19
mix_items.summary: Kindergarten is an important time in a child's life, during which children acquire and strengthen the skills needed to participate and learn in a school environment. Going to school regularly is an important part of this.

mix_items.title: New framework identifies 108 lysosomal disorders, nearly doubling recognized conditions
mix_items.summary: Lysosomal disorders can have devastating effects on patients but findings from a University of Sheffield-led collaborative study could support more precise diagnosis and help researchers identify shared targets for future treatments. The scientists have brought together the most comprehensive picture yet of rare metabolic disorders, identifying 108 conditions—almost double those originally understood to exist—bringing new hope for early diagnosis and new treatments.

mix_items.title: Newly found dendrite bottlenecks may reshape how neurons handle information
mix_items.summary: Neurons receive thousands of signals via tree-like extensions called dendrites. Until now, these dendrites were thought to be relatively smooth cables that conduct electrical signals to the cell body. An international research team led by University Hospital of Bonn (UKB), the University of Bonn and the DZNE has determined that this picture is incomplete.

mix_items.title: Social isolation in Australia has nearly doubled over two decades
mix_items.summary: Australians are becoming increasingly lonely and socially isolated, according to new University of Sydney research that found rates of social isolation nearly doubled over the past 23 years. Loneliness rates also increased over time, though more gradually than social isolation, with the sharpest impacts observed among vulnerable populations.

mix_items.title: Mosquito 'toilet' detects West Nile and first Hedwig-like virus found in the Americas
mix_items.summary: When public health researchers want to know whether diseases such as COVID-19 or polio are circulating in a community, they can look for genetic evidence in wastewater.

mix_items.title: Miniaturized bone marrow-on-a-chip tracks human immune cells as they build lasting antibody defenses
mix_items.summary: A scientific team has developed a laboratory model that reveals how antibody-producing plasma cells migrate, mature and survive within human bone marrow, a main location of long-lived antibody-producing plasma cells. The platform combines a lymph node-mimicking organoid with a tissue chip that mimics bone marrow, allowing scientists to observe key stages of plasma cell development that have been difficult to study in humans.

mix_items.title: Speedy electrons for brilliant laser light: Research paves the way for compact, inexpensive free-electron lasers
mix_items.summary: Extremely short, intense light flashes are in high demand to investigate atoms, molecules and new materials. Free-electron lasers (FELs) produce these flashes. But around the world, beam time available at large-scale user facilities is in short supply, and waiting times are long.

mix_items.title: School segregation endures in Baltimore region, report finds
mix_items.summary: Although public schools in Baltimore City are predominantly Black, the district is doing a better job of reducing segregation among its student body than suburban systems that are able to draw from more diverse populations, according to a new report from Johns Hopkins University.

mix_items.title: Examining the neural basis of socially anxious behaviors
mix_items.summary: People with social anxiety are especially sensitive to unpleasant outcomes, and this sensitivity contributes to their tendency to avoid social situations. Previous research has linked this learning bias to activity in specific brain regions. Hanjie Liu and Melle van der Molen of Leiden University extended this work by examining how communication between brain regions coordinates learning behavior in people with varying levels of social anxiety.

mix_items.title: AI updates can sometimes feel like breakups or losses, study finds
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence systems, particularly those powered by large language models and designed to communicate with users on a one-to-one basis, are increasingly used worldwide. Some of these systems, such as Replika, are also marketed as "AI companions" that can engage socially with humans and use emotional language.

mix_items.title: NASA Welcomes Djibouti as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
mix_items.summary: The Republic of Djibouti became the 72nd nation and eighth African country to sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony Monday at NASA Headquarters in Washington. The Artemis Accords are the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing transparency, safety, and coordination among nations as they explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. “Djibouti joins […]

mix_items.title: Gender representation key to women's job interest, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Women make up about half the U.S. population, yet remain a minority in many professions, such as politics, technology, science and academia.

mix_items.title: Young military veterans have higher 'forever chemical' levels than non-veterans
mix_items.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), often called forever chemicals because of their long-lasting presence in humans and the environment, are commonly found in consumer and industrial products. When Brown University researchers examined PFAS levels in the blood serum of U.S. military veterans, they found that younger veterans had higher PFAS concentrations and a higher prevalence of elevated PFAS levels compared with civilians of similar ages.

mix_items.title: Ghana's local architecture has adapted to change for centuries. It can teach us about climate resilience
mix_items.summary: When people discuss architecture in Ghana, attention often focuses on modern buildings: concrete houses, glass offices, shopping malls and ambitious urban developments. Yet across the country, another architectural tradition continues to offer lessons about how people have built and lived for generations.

mix_items.title: Early deafness may reshape the brain to devote more resources to peripheral vision
mix_items.summary: People with intact hearing can use sound as an alert system for events outside their direct line of sight. This seemingly puts those who have lost their hearing at a disadvantage. However, according to a new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the brains of people who lose their hearing at an early age may compensate by devoting more resources to developing better peripheral vision.

mix_items.title: Getting photons into shape for reliable quantum communication
mix_items.summary: The vast majority of modern quantum technologies—from quantum cryptography to the quantum internet to the quantum computer—rely on one essential element: the transmission of photons. Two qubits (two atoms, for example) exchange information: One qubit emits a photon, and the other qubit absorbs it.

mix_items.title: How the 2024 solar superstorm drained Earth's radiation belt
mix_items.summary: In May 2024, Earth experienced its most intense geomagnetic storm since the Halloween storms of 2003. This "superstorm" filled night skies in many parts of the world with colorful aurorae, and it disrupted some infrastructure, such as GPS signals used by agricultural equipment.

mix_items.title: Metabolic vulnerability identified that may affect heart development
mix_items.summary: The heart undergoes major changes during the first weeks of life. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet have now shown that a previously unknown metabolic vulnerability in mitochondria can disrupt heart development. The study, published in Science Advances, could improve our understanding of rare mitochondrial diseases that affect the heart.

mix_items.title: Why so few older Americans get counseling—and how it could help
mix_items.summary: People are living longer, reshaping what it means to grow old. By the late 2060s, an estimated 2.5 billion people worldwide will be 60 or older—more than the number of people who are under 18. The population ages 80 and older is expected to grow even faster, more than tripling between 2023 and 2060 to about 545 million.

mix_items.title: Engineered vesicles protect brain from bacterial toxin
mix_items.summary: Bacterial meningitis can cause severe brain damage even when patients receive antibiotic treatment promptly. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet have developed tiny biological vesicles that, in animal studies, were able to capture bacterial toxins, protect neurons, reduce inflammation and delay disease progression. The findings are published in the journal Journal of Extracellular Vesicles.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
mix_items.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

mix_items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
mix_items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

mix_items.title: New injectable treatment helps the brain rebuild after stroke
mix_items.summary: Duke researchers developed an injectable scaffold that helped stroke-damaged brains grow new blood vessels, support nerve regrowth, and recover movement in mice. The treatment appears to work partly by recruiting the body’s own immune cells, including neutrophils that may switch from damaging to helpful under the right conditions.

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
